text:
A design starts by naming the things your data is about. So take one sentence. Customers place orders for products. Circle the nouns... customers, orders, products. Each one's a candidate entity, a kind of thing worth tracking. Here's a test. Can there be many of these? Lots of customers, orders, products. An order's status, though? That just describes an order. It's a fact, not a thing.

Now, an entity is a TYPE of thing. The type becomes a table, and each real one, a row. Customers is the table. Ada is one row, because she's one real customer. Products get their own table. A product has a price... and a customer doesn't. So what do you need to remember about each one?

Those facts are attributes. An order has a status, a total, and the date it was placed. Each becomes a column. And every column has a domain, the values it's allowed to hold.

Say status is just text. Then anything goes in. Sent, shipped, ship in capitals, done... which ones mean the same? So narrow it. Four statuses, and no total below zero. Of those four spellings, only shipped gets in. And the status banana? Refused, with the name of the rule it broke.

But every rule like that is a claim. Cap a name at twenty characters, and you're claiming no name is longer. Johann Sebastian Bach is twenty-one. So be strict about what you control, like statuses. Go easy on what the world sends you, like names.

Keep one value per cell, too. Pack two phone numbers into one, and searching for either finds nothing. And a fact with details of its own, or lots of copies, like saved addresses? That's an entity too. Boxes and facts. Time to draw them.
